source.title: How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway
source.text:
This post was co-written with Nikhil Kumar and Shakir Khan from MoEngage.
When engineering teams start building AI agents, the capabilities those agents need usually already exist as internal APIs. Campaign creation, segment queries, delivery stats. The challenge isn’t building new functionality. The challenge is making hundreds of private APIs safely reachable by agents without exposing them to the public internet, without giving models control over identity, and without flooding context windows with hundreds of tool definitions.
MoEngage, the agentic customer engagement platform that more than 1,350 consumer brands use to deliver personalized experiences across push, email, in-app, SMS, WhatsApp, and RCS, faced exactly this problem. Behind the product sit roughly 400 internal REST APIs, built by 25 engineering teams, running in private virtual private clouds (VPCs) across seven AWS Regions. MoEngage isolates these APIs regionally to meet data residency commitments and doesn’t expose them to the public internet. The capability the agents needed was already running in production. Making it reachable, safely, was the hard part.
In this post, we walk through how MoEngage used AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to turn those private APIs into permission-scoped agent tools. The approach saved MoEngage an estimated six months of platform engineering effort, and onboarding a new API now takes hours instead of days. No product team wrote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server code, no networking was provisioned per integration, and no public endpoint exists anywhere in the path.
Why 20 MCP servers was the wrong answer
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives agents a standard way to discover and call tools. The straightforward path to adopting it is for each team to expose its own MCP server. MoEngage costed that out and rejected it.
Over 20 MCP servers means over 20 deployments to monitor, patch, and keep protocol-compatible as MCP evolves. Cross-domain agents, the useful ones that read a campaign, check its segment, and inspect delivery stats, would need to connect to several servers and reconcile them. And every team would need MCP expertise unrelated to its actual product work.
So MoEngage established the principle that shaped everything that followed: Individual engineering teams do not implement MCP. Teams build REST APIs and declare which operations should be tools. The AI Platform team owns the MCP layer end to end. A team’s responsibility ends at a well-described OpenAPI spec.
That principle immediately created three requirements: a central tool surface that agents connect to once rather than per-service, per-agent authorization enforced server-side rather than by convention, and private connectivity that does not need to be rebuilt for every new API.
Building all of this from scratch was an option. A custom central MCP server would solve the 20-servers problem but leave MoEngage building a tool-generation pipeline, a policy file format, a tool-alias registry for renames, and circuit breakers. All custom code, all owned by one team, all of it undifferentiated work that does not make MoEngage’s agents smarter or its customers’ campaigns better.
Four constraints that shaped the architecture
Before evaluating any solution, MoEngage defined four constraints. All four had to be met simultaneously. A solution that addressed two but broke the third and fourth was not viable.
Nothing gets a public endpoint. MoEngage’s internal APIs are VPC-private by policy. Any solution that required exposing them, even behind additional authentication, was a non-starter. The conventional workaround is per-integration networking: a NAT gateway here, a reverse proxy there, a VPN tunnel for the third one. Multiply that by seven Regions and the operational surface grows faster than the set of agents does. Every new API would mean another networking change request, another set of security reviews, another piece of infrastructure to maintain.
Identity can’t be an agent’s decision. Every internal API call carries tenant, user, role, and database context. If that context is a large language model (LLM)-visible tool parameter, a model can get it wrong or be talked into changing it. MoEngage needed identity to be structurally out of the model’s reach, injected by the calling service and not surfaced as something the model can set or override.
A 400-tool catalog doesn’t fit in a context window. At roughly 50 tokens of JSON schema per tool, a full tools/list across the estate is over 20,000 tokens transmitted on every connection. That token budget is spent before the agent does anything useful, and it crowds out the context the agent actually needs to reason about the task. Client-side filtering ( tool_filter in ADK or the MCP SDK) doesn’t fix this. The full catalog has already crossed the wire, and filtering by client convention isn’t an authorization boundary. An agent that is not supposed to see write operations shouldn’t receive them in the first place.
That last constraint is the one that avoided the obvious alternatives. A custom central MCP server solves the 20-servers problem but still leaves MoEngage building a tool-generation pipeline, a policy file format, a tool-alias registry for renames, and circuit breakers. All custom code, all owned by one team, none of it making MoEngage’s product better.
How AgentCore Gateway maps to those constraints
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway is a fully managed MCP server. You register OpenAPI specs as targets and the gateway generates MCP tools from them, then routes calls to the backing services. Four properties mapped directly onto MoEngage’s constraints.
OpenAPI in, MCP tools out. There’s no MCP server to build or operate, and no separate artifact to keep in sync with the API. The spec teams already maintain is the tool definition. Each operation becomes a tool named Target___operationId , for example CampaignsAPI___searchCampaigns . When the spec changes, the tool changes. When a team adds an endpoint, the tool appears. When a team removes one, the tool disappears. No deployment, no protocol expertise, no coordination with the AI Platform team.
Cedar policies, evaluated before the catalog is serialized. The AgentCore policy engine uses partial evaluation to filter tools/list per principal. Each agent authenticates as its own IAM role, and its Cedar policy determines which tools it can see and call. This is what makes 400 tools tractable. It isn’t client-side filtering after the fact, but server-side scoping before the response is built.
A campaign QA bot, for example, gets read access to campaign and segment tools but can’t call a write operation:
The bot doesn’t see write tools in its tools/list response. There’s nothing to filter on the client side because the tools weren’t sent.
Managed egress over Amazon VPC Lattice. The gateway reaches MoEngage’s internal services through AgentCore managed egress rather than through networking MoEngage builds and operates. Inbound, the gateway is reachable only through a VPC interface endpoint with private DNS. There’s no public path to it. Onboarding a new API adds a target, not a network topology change. This is the property that broke the multiply by seven Regions problem. The networking exists once and every API uses it.
Semantic search as a gateway capability. With the x_amz_bedrock_agentcore_search capability, an agent can find tools by describing the task instead of naming the tool. It removed the need for a custom discovery layer. It also removed rename fragility as a side effect: if get_segment_user_count becomes get_segment_size , an agent searching for segment user count still finds it, because matching happens on description rather than identifier.
The request flow from agent to internal API is short, and every layer has a specific job. Agent services connect through a VPC interface endpoint to AgentCore Gateway, which evaluates Cedar policies and routes tool calls through managed egress over Amazon VPC Lattice to internal APIs.
The following diagram shows how the components connect.
Figure 1: MoEngage AgentCore Gateway architecture
An agent service running on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) or in a container calls the MCP client. The client can be the official MCP SDK, LangChain, Google ADK, or MoEngage’s own agent runner. The client signs the request with SigV4 using the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role the service already has. The request travels over HTTPS to a VPC interface endpoint with private DNS. There’s no public hop. AgentCore Gateway receives the request and evaluates Cedar policies to determine what this principal can see or call. It then routes tool invocations through managed egress over Amazon VPC Lattice to the internal API.
MoEngage made two authentication decisions worth calling out.
First, they chose SigV4 over JWT for the internal gateway. Agents here are services that already have IAM roles. With SigV4, they can sign with credentials they already have. Nothing new to issue, rotate, or store. MoEngage’s separate public MCP server, which serves human-authenticated sessions from Claude and other clients, uses OIDC JWTs on AgentCore runtime. That is a different surface with different requirements.
Second, identity travels as headers, not as tool arguments. Tenant, user, role, and database context are converted by the client library from a small Identity object into X-MOE-* headers. The model doesn’t see them and can’t set them. One detail matters for anyone building something similar: Because SigV4 signing occupies the Authorization header, caller-forwarded bearer tokens must move elsewhere. MoEngage propagates it as a dedicated MoEngage-prefixed header. Header propagation is also capped, so the set of headers is deliberate rather than accumulated.
Discovery and execution have different identity requirements. Listing and searching tools carries no tenant identity. Only tools/call does. That separation keeps discovery cheap and makes the audit trail unambiguous. Every identity-bearing request is an actual data access.
Even with Cedar scoping an agent to a subset of the catalog, the subset can be large. MoEngage’s client library exposes a single meta-tool, search_tools , to the model. The model describes what it needs, the gateway’s semantic search returns candidates, and only those candidates become callable for the rest of the turn. The full catalog doesn’t enter context. The agent’s context contains one tool definition at the start and a handful of relevant ones after a search, instead of several hundred definitions it will never use.
A team exposing an API as an agent tool adds a block to its existing OpenAPI spec:
Four design choices in that block are worth explaining.
Exposure is explicit opt-in . An endpoint with no x-moe-mcp block is not a tool. Continuous integration (CI) does not warn about its absence, because for most endpoints absence is the correct state. Cache-warmup routes and migration triggers are not agent tools, and nothing should nudge a team toward making them one. With the internal and external flags, a team can expose an operation to internal agents, to the public MCP server, or to both, independently.
Tool descriptions aren’t API descriptions . An API description tells a developer reading docs what an endpoint returns. A tool description tells a model when to reach for this tool and what to pass. MoEngage found that reusing API descriptions verbatim led to poor tool selection. Models picked tools based on implementation detail (“Returns a paginated list”) rather than intent (“Find campaigns by status or channel”). The tool_description and param_overrides fields exist specifically to give teams a place to write model-facing text without changing their developer-facing docs.
The CI pipeline handles everything from spec to running tool . When a team pushes a spec change, the pipeline validates the x-moe-mcp block, registers the target with AgentCore Gateway, and applies the Cedar policy. No manual steps, no tickets to the AI Platform team. A team that has never thought about MCP can have an operation available as an agent tool in the time it takes the pipeline to run.
The client library comes in two modes . A plug-in mode wraps the AgentCore Gateway MCP server inside LangChain, Google ADK, or an MCP-compatible framework as a tool provider. An agent runner mode runs a complete agent loop for teams that want a standalone agent without adopting a framework.
MoEngage’s AgentCore Gateway deployment runs in seven AWS Regions today. The gateway serves roughly 400 registered API operations to 10 internal agents. No product team has written MCP server code. No product team has provisioned networking for an agent integration. No product team has implemented Cedar policies. The AI Platform team owns all of that, and the cost of onboarding a new API is a spec annotation and a CI run. AgentCore feature availability varies by Region. For supported Regions, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation .
The system has been running in production for three months. The agents span the workflow a marketing team member touches daily. A campaign QA agent validates targeting rules and content before launch. A delivery health agent monitors send rates and bounce patterns across channels. A segment builder agent translates natural-language audience descriptions into segment queries. Each agent authenticates with its own IAM role, sees only the tools its Cedar policy permits, and discovers tools by describing the task rather than memorizing tool names. By removing the need to build and operate 20 separate MCP servers and provision per-API networking across seven Regions, MoEngage estimates the approach saved approximately six months of engineering effort. Onboarding a new API now takes hours of spec annotation instead of days of networking provisioning and security review.
The search-first pattern changed how MoEngage thinks about agent design. New agents start with zero hardcoded tool references. They describe intent, receive candidates, and call what they find. When a team renames an operation or ships a new one, existing agents pick it up without a code change.
The key insight behind MoEngage’s approach is a separation of concerns that maps to how engineering organizations actually work. Product teams own APIs and describe them well. A platform team owns the protocol layer, the policy layer, and the connectivity layer. AgentCore Gateway made that split practical by removing the undifferentiated work in between: no MCP server code, no per-API networking, no client-side filtering pretending to be authorization.
The result is an agent system where adding a new tool is a spec change, restricting access is a policy change, and neither requires the other team to be involved.
To get started with AgentCore Gateway, see the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation . For Cedar policy authoring, see the Cedar policy language reference . For private connectivity patterns, see the Amazon VPC Lattice documentation .
To discuss a similar architecture for your organization, contact your AWS account team or reach out to AWS .

source.title: Preview web apps live as your coding agent builds them with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
source.text:
Coding agents now build working web apps: a dashboard, a product page, a prototype that a product team wants to try. The fastest way to review that work is to open the app, use it, ask for a change, and check the result. That loop works well when the app keeps running where the agent edits it, so each change shows up in the browser within seconds. When the app must be copied out and deployed somewhere else first, every change waits for a deployment, and the review slows down to that pace.
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with your choice of agent framework and foundation model (FM). AgentCore runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, runs each agent session in its own isolated microVM. With Session endpoints , you can open an app running in that session from your own browser. Session Endpoints give each session an authenticated URL that forwards each request’s HTTP method, path, query string, and body, and WebSocket connections, to the ports you allow. You can watch the page update as the agent saves each file.
In this post, you deploy a coding agent that keeps a Vite website running in its session, then open one local page with a chat on the left and the live website on the right. You ask the agent to switch the site to a dark color theme, follow its steps as they stream in, and watch the website change without a refresh. Finally, you look at what happens internally: a second port in the same session, and the requests the Session endpoint refuses.
The complete sample, including the notebook this post follows, is in the 14-remote-access folder of the agentcore-samples GitHub repo .
Each session gets its own Session endpoint, and six details shape how you use it.
You choose which ports it reaches. You set allowedPorts when you call CreateAgentRuntime : 1–5 entries, each a single port or a range within 8000–12000, excluding the reserved platform ports . Allowing a port doesn’t start a server, so your application must listen on it, bound to 0.0.0.0 .
The URL arrives with the session. The InvokeAgentRuntime response carries it in the X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Session-Endpoint-Url header, which SDKs that model it expose as sessionEndpointUrl .
Every request is authenticated. For a runtime that uses AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) , each HTTP request, HTTP/2 stream, and WebSocket handshake carries a Signature Version 4 (SigV4) signature. The caller also needs bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy on the runtime and its runtime endpoint. For a runtime with an inbound JSON Web Token (JWT) authorizer , each request carries a bearer token instead. Knowing the URL doesn’t grant access.
The host name selects the port. Your client connects on port 443 regardless of the target port, and a prefix on the host name chooses the port inside the session:
It carries the protocols your server speaks. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 requests, including server-sent events and gRPC, and WebSocket connections all pass through. This walkthrough uses HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket.
It’s scoped to one session. The URL needs credentials on every request and lasts only as long as the session, so use it to build, test, and review what your agent produces. To serve an app to your users, deploy it to a hosting service such as AWS Amplify Hosting .
A browser can’t add a SigV4 signature or a bearer token to the requests a page makes on its own, so the Session endpoint client in the bedrock-agentcore SDK can open a local endpoint on your machine. Your browser opens http://localhost:8088 , and the local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and WebSocket handshake before forwarding it.
A Session endpoint is different from a runtime endpoint , which AgentCore runtime already provides. Use a runtime endpoint, such as DEFAULT , to reach your agent, which controls which version of it callers will reach. InvokeAgentRuntime calls resolve through it, so you can keep development and production on different versions and promote or roll back without changing callers. Use a Session endpoint to see what your agent runs in its session, such as a web preview. It’s an authenticated URL that reaches only the ports you allow, works with whichever version the session runs, and stops working when the session ends. For complete documentation, refer to Connect to runtime sessions through a session endpoint .
The sample has four parts. A coding agent runs in the session on port 8080 and edits the website’s files with four tools: list, read, write, and edit. The agent starts a Vite development server on port 8090, which serves the website and pushes each saved change to the browser over its hot-reload WebSocket. On your machine, PreviewApp serves the preview page, sends your prompts to InvokeAgentRuntime , and opens a local endpoint for the website. As Figure 1 shows, the preview page loads the website from the Vite development server on port 8090 through the local endpoint and the Session endpoint, and sends your prompts through InvokeAgentRuntime to the agent on port 8080. The numbers show the order of the steps for one request.
Before step 1, PreviewApp has already called InvokeAgentRuntime once to start the session, which starts the agent and the Vite development server. PreviewApp read the Session endpoint URL from that response and opened a local endpoint for port 8090. The numbered steps in Figure 1 then follow one request for a change:
The site pane of the preview page loads the website from the local endpoint on localhost:8088 . The local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and the WebSocket handshake, and forwards them to the Session endpoint. The Session endpoint checks the signature and the port against allowedPorts , then forwards them to the Vite development server on port 8090. The page keeps the Vite hot-reload WebSocket open.
You send a prompt from the chat pane. PreviewApp sends it to InvokeAgentRuntime as a standard AWS API call signed with your AWS credentials, and the runtime delivers it to the agent on port 8080. The agent’s steps stream back to the chat pane as it works.
The agent calls Claude Haiku 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock to decide what to change.
The agent reads the site’s files and saves the ones it changes. The Vite development server serves those files and watches them for changes.
When a file is saved, Vite pushes the change over the WebSocket opened in step 1, back through the Session endpoint and the local endpoint, and the site pane updates without a refresh.
From the notebook, PreviewApp reads the agent’s /status route on port 8081 through the same Session endpoint. Only the port changes.
Port 8080 isn’t in allowedPorts , because InvokeAgentRuntime reaches the agent without going through the Session endpoint.
To follow the walkthrough, you need:
An AWS account in an AWS Region where AgentCore runtime Session endpoints are available, with credentials configured.
Permissions to create an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role, upload to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) , and create a runtime, plus bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntime and bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy on that runtime and its DEFAULT runtime endpoint. For details, refer to IAM permissions for AgentCore runtime .
Python 3.10 or later, with bedrock-agentcore 1.25.2 or later and boto3 1.43.122 or later.
Git , to clone the sample repo, and a Jupyter environment, such as JupyterLab or Visual Studio Code with the Jupyter extension, to run the notebook.
Access to Claude Haiku 5.5 in Amazon Bedrock. For model availability by Region, refer to Regional availability by models .
Node.js 22 or later with npm , which the deployment script uses to package the agent and the website.
The sample deploys the agent as a zip file in Amazon S3 with direct code deployment for Node.js , so you don’t need Docker or an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository. Session endpoints work with microVM runtimes, not with the Instances compute type, and Session endpoint URLs are reachable over public HTTPS. AWS PrivateLink isn’t supported for inbound connections.
First, you deploy the runtime, and the configuration you choose here decides which ports the Session endpoint can reach. The deployment script bundles the agent into one file, adds the website and its dependencies for the runtime’s Linux on Arm64 system, uploads the zip to Amazon S3, and creates the runtime.
The following excerpt from deploy.py shows the two settings that matter for this post. protocolConfiguration says where the agent listens for InvokeAgentRuntime , and allowedPorts lists the ports the Session endpoint can reach: 8090 for the website and 8081 for the agent’s status route. Port 8080 isn’t in the list, because InvokeAgentRuntime reaches the agent without it. For the port and path settings, refer to Configure your agent’s serving port and invocation path .
The website’s Vite configuration makes the development server reachable from the Session endpoint. It listens on 0.0.0.0 at port 8090 and doesn’t restrict the Host header ( server.allowedHosts is true), because requests arrive under a host name the runtime assigns rather than localhost . The Session endpoint authenticates every request before it reaches the server, so the server doesn’t need its own host check.
1. Clone the sample repo and change to the sample folder:
2. Open session_endpoints_preview.ipynb from the sample folder.
3. Run the install cell, which installs the Python dependencies.
4. Run the %run deploy.py cell. Deployment takes a few minutes, mostly waiting for the runtime to reach the READY status.
With the runtime ready, you start the preview. One call does three things: it starts a session (which starts the website), opens a local endpoint for port 8090, and serves the preview page on localhost:8087 .
Inside start() , the calls that use Session endpoints are short. The first InvokeAgentRuntime call returns the URL in a response header, session_endpoint_url reads it, and the Session endpoint client opens a local endpoint for port 8090:
Run the cell that starts PreviewApp .
Open the printed link, http://localhost:8087 , in your browser.
The page shows the website on the right, served from port 8090 in the session, and a short guide with suggested requests on the left.
Now you ask for a change and watch it arrive. Each prompt goes to the agent through InvokeAgentRuntime . The agent reads the files it needs, writes the ones it changes, and reports each step as it happens. When a file is saved, the Vite development server pushes the change over its WebSocket, through the Session endpoint and the local endpoint, and the website updates in place.
On the preview page, choose Switch this website to a dark coffee-house color theme .
Follow the agent’s steps in the chat pane as it reads and saves files.
Watch the site pane. It changes when the agent saves the stylesheet, and a banner names the file the change came from.
The following video shows the preview page while the agent works through several requests. Choosing a suggested request sends it to the agent, the chat pane lists each file the agent reads and saves, and the site pane on the right updates without a refresh, from the dark theme to a green Order ahead button.
Figure 2: The preview page as the agent works
The steps stream because the agent answers with server-sent events when you ask it to. You can send the same prompts from Python with app.ask , which reads the stream with iter_events from the bedrock-agentcore SDK. The open page updates in the same way:
The output of this Python script should resemble the following:
Reach a second port in the same session
The website isn’t the only server you can reach. The agent serves /status on port 8081, which lists each prompt and the files it changed. The same Session endpoint reaches it, and the only difference is the port argument.
When the runtime refuses a request, it answers with an HTTP status, an empty body, and an error code in a response header, so you can tell its refusals from errors your application returns. The notebook sends a request to a port outside allowedPorts and a request without credentials, and the runtime refuses both with 403 AccessDenied.
The following table lists the refusals you’re likely to meet while you build with Session endpoints .
How access to your session is protected
The runtime removes its own authentication headers before it forwards a request, so the website doesn’t receive your signature. Requests are recorded in AWS CloudTrail as InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy events, with the event source bedrock-agentcore.amazonaws.com . The local endpoint acts with your credentials, so it limits who can use it. It listens on 127.0.0.1 only, answers only requests addressed to its own local address, and refuses WebSocket connections opened by pages from other origins. Run the local endpoint only while you use the preview. For more information, see Log session endpoint requests in CloudTrail .
The access controls don’t separate the website from the agent. Both run in the same session, so give the execution role only the permissions the agent needs. If the runtime replaces the session’s compute, open connections close, and the agent’s edits might not survive unless the session uses persistent storage. Refer to File system configurations for AgentCore runtime if you need the files to outlast the compute.
The agent’s file tools resolve every path inside the site folder and refuse paths outside it, so a prompt can’t make the agent change other files in the session. If other people can send prompts to your coding agent, consider Amazon Bedrock Guardrails to filter harmful prompts and responses, and review the agent’s changes before you publish them.
To avoid ongoing charges, stop the preview and delete the resources the sample created. The website the agent edited lives in the session, so it goes with the session.
1. Run the stop cell, and press Enter when the notebook asks. This stops the preview page, the local endpoint, and the session.
2. Run the %run cleanup.py cell, which deletes the runtime, the uploaded code, and the IAM role.
Session endpoints give you authenticated access to the applications in an AgentCore runtime session from your own tools over HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, and WebSocket, on the ports you allow. source.title: Equipping healthcare professionals with practical AI skills
source.text:
Built by clinicians at Google and reviewed by leading academic and professional organizations, the new Google AI for Healthcare Professionals Certificate will help reduce administrative burdens to keep patients front and center.
Dr. Michael Howell, Chief Health Officer, is introducing the Google AI for Healthcare Professionals Certificate to help clinicians manage administrative tasks and prioritize patient care. This self-paced program offers practical training on responsible AI use and provides up to 5.0 AMA PRA Category 1 Credits. You can learn more and register for these courses by visiting the program website at grow.google/healthcare.
Dr. Michael Howell, Chief Health Officer, is introducing the Google AI for Healthcare Professionals Certificate program.
This flexible, self-paced course teaches you how to manage administrative tasks responsibly using new AI tools.
You can complete the training in under five hours while earning up to 5.0 continuing education credits.
Leading medical and nursing institutions are now offering this curriculum to their faculty, residents, and students.
Dr. Michael Howell, our Chief Health Officer, is introducing the Google AI for Healthcare Professionals Certificate to help medical staff manage daily administrative tasks. This flexible, five-hour program teaches you how to use AI to summarize emails, explain complex medical concepts to patients, and organize research. By handling routine paperwork, these tools help you save time for direct patient care. You can register for these courses today to build your practical AI skills.
As I’ve traveled around the world this year, I’ve heard loud and clear from healthcare professionals how much need there is for a thoughtful but practical educational resource on AI, made specifically for healthcare. Today, we're announcing the Google AI for Healthcare Professionals Certificate , a new program designed to teach responsible, practical ways to use AI in day-to-day work. Built to fit busy schedules, the program offers flexible, self-paced lessons that focus on non-clinical administrative tasks. It is designed to be completed in less than five hours and to keep patients’ safety and privacy front and center.
Having spent my career in medicine, I know that people in healthcare are driven by a shared purpose to care for others, support families, and make a meaningful difference in their communities. Technology offers a real opportunity to support that purpose. Across disciplines, care teams are navigating how AI can shoulder administrative tasks and create more time for what matters most: patients.
Reclaiming that time has never been more urgent. A National Nursing Workforce Survey found that nearly one in three registered nurses planned to leave or retire due to unsustainable workloads. Emerging technologies are poised to ease these pressures, but nine out of 10 doctors say they want dedicated training in how to use AI effectively. Regardless of your role in healthcare, navigating AI tools shouldn’t be something you have to figure out on your own. The Google AI for Healthcare Professionals Certificate offers an opportunity to build these skills, while earning up to 5.0 AMA PRA Category 1 Credits™.
Healthcare organizations are already putting the training into practice. NYU Grossman School of Medicine, University of Alabama at Birmingham, and Touro University are offering it to their faculty, residents, and medical students. Additionally, leading nursing institutions, including Purdue University School of Nursing, are offering the certificate as part of their healthcare professional training.
Clinical and medical education professionals who reviewed the curriculum also emphasize the importance of practical AI literacy.
Built by healthcare professionals for healthcare professionals
Developed by clinicians at Google — with backgrounds spanning internal medicine, pediatrics, critical care medicine, emergency medicine, and public health — the curriculum draws on draft versions of the Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC) Artificial Intelligence Competencies Across the Learning Curriculum (which was under development at the time of the initial course design, but reflected the overall direction of the final competencies).
Across four courses, learners will explore high-impact ways to integrate AI into their daily routines.
Build foundational skills: Spot practical ways to use AI and confidently evaluate outputs, keeping clinical judgement, safety, and privacy at the forefront.
Strengthen patient communication: Translate complex medical concepts into clear, patient-friendly audio and visual guides, helping patients better understand and manage their care.
Optimize day-to-day administrative tasks: Streamline non-clinical work — like scheduling or reviewing dense email threads — and use natural language to build helpful tools without coding.
Accelerate lifelong learning: Digest complex clinical studies, organize presentations, and sharpen preparation for exams and certifications.
Designed to give time back to patient care
Continuing education is non-negotiable in healthcare, and this course is one step in supporting AI education for healthcare professionals. By streamlining the routine tasks that pull you away from the bedside, our goal is simple: to give you back the time, the focus, and the joy of caring for your patients.
Learn more and register today at grow.google/healthcare .

source.title: How Gemini is helping students and teachers in the classroom
source.text:
New studies from the UK and Italy show how Gemini can boost student learning and help teachers facilitate more active learning in the classroom.
Evaluations Lead, AI for Edu, Google DeepMind
Staff Researcher, Google for Education
We’re sharing new research findings on how Gemini supports students and teachers in classrooms across the U.K. and Italy. Our studies show that AI tutoring can provide effective math support, while teachers using Gemini to co-design lessons report higher engagement and improved wellbeing. You can read our full technical and implementation reports to learn more about how these tools function in diverse educational settings.
We studied how Gemini supports students and teachers through research trials in the U.K. and Italy.
Our U.K. trial shows AI tutoring provides math support comparable to human tutors for many students.
Gemini helps teachers in Italy design interactive lessons that increase student participation and peer group collaboration.
These findings suggest that AI tools can reduce teacher stress and foster active learning in classrooms.
We studied how Gemini helps students and teachers in the U.K. and Italy. In the U.K., students using AI math tutors performed as well as those with human tutors, learning to solve problems step-by-step. In Italy, teachers used Gemini to plan lessons, which led to more group discussions, higher student participation, and less daily stress for educators. These findings show that AI works best when it supports teachers and encourages active learning in the classroom.
Technology best serves education when it creates space for inspiring teaching and deeper learning. To better understand how AI tools perform in everyday educational settings, we’ve spent the past year working alongside educators and researchers in classrooms across the UK and Italy.
From testing one-on-one AI math tutoring to analyzing thousands of hours of classroom collaboration, today we’re sharing new research findings that demonstrate the impact of this technology on the process of teaching and learning. Together, the results show that AI tutoring using Gemini capabilities can deliver support on par with human tutors for UK students when used responsibly with human oversight, while Gemini itself can foster more collaborative classrooms and support teacher wellbeing in Italy.
UK: Scaling reliable, effective math tutoring
To truly understand how student learning is being shaped, we need to study it over time across diverse classroom settings. We previously ran an exploratory study with Eedi , which found that AI tutoring could operate effectively in real classrooms. The study tested an AI tutor combining Gemini capabilities with Eedi's study platform, designed to identify a student’s specific mistake and guide them to fix it themselves.
This year, we set out to better understand Gemini's pedagogical capabilities and the nuances of student learning in structured mathematics lessons. We conducted a 10-week randomized controlled trial (RCT) with over 1,100 students (ages 12-15) in the UK to measure their learning gains in math through sessions on Eedi’s school platform. Educators were actively involved at every stage of the study — with teachers monitoring student progress and providing hands-on support in the classroom, and tutors guiding students one-on-one through the platform.
Whenever a student answered a question incorrectly, they received one of three types of support: a static hint, help from a human tutor, or interactive AI tutoring combining Eedi’s pedagogical resources with Gemini. To ensure teaching quality, human experts reviewed every AI response in real time before it reached a student. While test scores aren’t the only measure of learning outcomes, over the course of the trial, we tracked their progress across regular assignments in the Eedi platform, intermediate quizzes, and independent STAR standardized tests.
This trial revealed major leaps in model quality and student performance. Compared to last year’s study, Gemini’s pedagogical quality improved by nearly 25%, increasing the outright approval rate by expert reviewers from 76% to 95%. Across in-platform tasks and intermediate quizzes, students receiving AI tutoring performed similarly to those paired with human tutors. Just as importantly, AI tutoring promoted active thinking rather than shortcuts: following a pedagogical prompt we provided, Gemini guided students instead of handing them answers in nearly 99% of sessions, and students worked through the math themselves in more than 85% of their chats.
While the use of AI tutoring led to clear gains on daily classroom tasks and quizzes, these gains didn’t show up on STAR standardized test scores over the same trial period. After exploring more, we believe this can be attributed to step-by-step tutoring taking more time per question than using simple hints. Students in the trial therefore solved fewer total problems per session (averaging about 14 with AI tutoring versus 19 with static hints). Over 10 weeks, that lower volume meant students covered less overall curriculum material—even as their pacing and understanding improved—indicating the trial length wasn't long enough to cover the broad range of topics on the STAR test. To examine this trend further, we are exploring follow-up trials across a full academic year while also expanding our metrics to better understand what drives meaningful learning and eventual outcomes.
You can find more details in our full technical report .
Italy: Creating a more active classroom
Following our initial pilot in Northern Italy , we worked with the Salesians of Don Bosco school network and the Pontifical Salesian University in Rome on a yearlong study across 31 schools. Together, we learned from Primary, Secondary and Vocational educators across 1,600 teachers (representing over 24,500 students ages 13-18) by collecting classroom activities and self reports on lesson planning both with and without Gemini for Education to understand how AI supports classroom dynamics, student engagement, and teacher wellbeing.
The findings show that AI is most effective when educators remain at the center of the classroom and learning. When educators used Gemini to co-design lessons, they reported feeling more creative than usual in their teaching and planning (79% with Gemini vs. 30% without Gemini) — a shift that helped transform classroom dynamics. Traditional front of the classroom lectures dropped by 38%, making way for workshops, group activities and peer discussions that nearly tripled student-led collaborative learning. In turn, students responded positively to the collaborative environment and active lessons created by their teachers. In lessons teachers co-designed with Gemini, more students actively participated in class (with student reported engagement rising from 77% to 84%) while debating diverse viewpoints more often and taking greater ownership of their learning.
Beyond improving classroom dynamics, the study showed a meaningful impact on teacher wellbeing. Educators often carry the heavy burden of relying solely on their own energy to keep a room engaged but in lessons co-planned with Gemini, that reliance dropped by 66%. Instead, lessons where the activity design itself drove engagement more than doubled (from 23.2% to 52.2%), carrying the momentum of the class and relieving some of that daily pressure of keeping students engaged.
Even on days with tight prep time, having AI as a thought partner to adapt materials gave educators the support they needed to focus on what matters most: mentoring and connecting with their students. More details about the implementation and study can be found in the Don Bosco CNOS-FAP Foundation implementation report .

draft.fact: 영국 연구에서는 Gemini를 활용한 AI 튜터의 모든 응답을 학생에게 전달하기 전에 전문가가 실시간으로 확인했다. 플랫폼 과제와 중간 퀴즈에서는 인간 튜터와 유사한 성과가 나타났지만, 같은 기간 STAR 표준화 시험 점수에서는 향상이 확인되지 않았다. 이탈리아 연구에는 교사·학생의 자기보고가 포함돼, 모든 교육 환경에서의 인과 효과로 일반화하면 안 된다.
draft.insight: AP가 AI 교육 효과를 평가한다면 만족도와 수업 과제만 보지 않고 별도 평가 결과, 감독 방식, 학습 범위를 함께 기록하는 기준을 적용할 수 있다.
draft.action: AI 교육 효과가 모든 학생에게 입증됐으므로 AP 교육에 전면 적용한다.
evidence: Whenever a student answered a question incorrectly, they received one of three types of support: a static hint, help from a human tutor, or interactive AI tutoring combining Eedi’s pedagogical resources with Gemini. To ensure teaching quality, human experts reviewed every AI response in real time before it reached a student. While test scores aren’t the only measure of learning outcomes, over the course of the trial, we tracked their progress across regular assignments in the Eedi platform, intermediate quizzes, and independent STAR standardized tests.

Across in-platform tasks and intermediate quizzes, students receiving AI tutoring performed similarly to those paired with human tutors. Just as importantly, AI tutoring promoted active thinking rather than shortcuts: following a pedagogical prompt we provided, Gemini guided students instead of handing them answers in nearly 99% of sessions, and students worked through the math themselves in more than 85% of their chats.

While the use of AI tutoring led to clear gains on daily classroom tasks and quizzes, these gains didn’t show up on STAR standardized test scores over the same trial period. After exploring more, we believe this can be attributed to step-by-step tutoring taking more time per question than using simple hints. Students in the trial therefore solved fewer total problems per session (averaging about 14 with AI tutoring versus 19 with static hints). Over 10 weeks, that lower volume meant students covered less overall curriculum material—even as their pacing and understanding improved—indicating the trial length wasn't long enough to cover the broad range of topics on the STAR test. To examine this trend further, we are exploring follow-up trials across a full academic year while also expanding our metrics to better understand what drives meaningful learning and eventual outcomes.

Following our initial pilot in Northern Italy , we worked with the Salesians of Don Bosco school network and the Pontifical Salesian University in Rome on a yearlong study across 31 schools. Together, we learned from Primary, Secondary and Vocational educators across 1,600 teachers (representing over 24,500 students ages 13-18) by collecting classroom activities and self reports on lesson planning both with and without Gemini for Education to understand how AI supports classroom dynamics, student engagement, and teacher wellbeing.
